overview.description: Laus (German for 'Louse'), also known as 'BÃ¶se Dame' (Evil Queen) or 'Graue Laus', is a traditional German avoidance trick-taking game. Played with a 32-card German or French deck, it is a precursor to games like Hearts and Black Maria. The primary goal is to avoid capturing the Queen of Spades (the 'Louse'), which carries a heavy point penalty. Players must follow suit, aiming to dump high-value cards on their opponents.

history.origins: Dates to the early 19th century in Northern Germany. It shares mechanics with the broader European family of 'Black Maria' and 'Hearts' games, which all evolved from earlier penalty trick-taking games.
timeline: 1850s: Rules for 'BÃ¶se Dame' emerge in German recreational gaming books.
1900s: The name 'Laus' becomes popular for the avoidance variant played with Skat cards (32-card deck).
Present: Remains a common trick-taking game for teaching counting and suit-management to beginners in German-speaking regions.
history.evolution: The game evolved to have a very high penalty for the Queen of Spades (typically 50 points) compared to the point-value of other cards, making it the central focus of every round. This 'one bad card' mechanic influenced the development of Hearts.
history.cultural: In some German regions, the loser of a game is called the 'Lausebengel' (Naughty Boy). The game is often used to introduce children to trick-taking mechanics before teaching more complex games like Skat or Doppelkopf.

setup.players: Optimal for 3 or 4 players. Can be played with 2 with modifications.
setup.deck: 32 cards (standard 52 minus 2-6). Use a Piquet or Skat deck, or remove cards 2-6 from a standard deck. No trumps.
setup.dealing: All 32 cards are dealt out equally. For 4 players: 8 cards each. For 3 players: 10 cards each with 2 discarded (or dealt 10-11-11).

rules.objective: Score the fewest points. Avoid capturing the Queen of Spades (50 points) and minimize capture of other point cards.
rules.gameplay: Standard trick-taking: 1. Must follow suit if possible. 2. If void in led suit, may play any card. 3. Highest card of the led suit wins the trick. 4. There are no trumps. 5. Winner leads to the next trick.
keyRules: Ace = 11 points, Ten = 10 points, King = 4 points, Queen = 3 points, Jack = 2 points.
The Queen of Spades can be played at any time once a player is void in the led suit, even if they hold other spades (the 'Laus' rule).
Game ends when a player reaches 100 or 150 points (agreed beforehand). Lowest score wins.

strategy.basic: Dump your high-value Spades! If you have the Queen of Spades, you MUST try to discard it when someone else leads a high Spade (Ace or King). If you don't have the Queen, avoid leading Spades until you know who has it.
strategy.intermediate: Suit Exhaustion: Choose one suit where you have very few cards (e.g., only one Heart). Void that suit early by playing your card when you can. Once you are void, you have a safe 'dumping ground' for the Queen of Spades or high Tens when those suits are led.
strategy.advanced: The Ace Shield: If you hold a high Ace, don't lead that suit early. Save it for the end of the game when others are more likely to have discarded their low cards, forcing you to win multiple high-point cards at once. Track which point cards have been playedâ€”if the Queen hasn't appeared yet and you're holding the King of Spades, be very careful about leading Spades.
tips: Counting the Spades is mandatory. If the King and Ace of Spades haven't been played yet, and you have the Queen, do NOT lead Spades yourself.
Aces (11 pts) and Tens (10 pts) are nearly as dangerous as the Queen in a close game; don't capture them unless you have no lower cards of that suit.
If you must win a trick, try to win one with minimal point cards in it.
Watch for the 'dangerous' playersâ€”those who are void in multiple suits can dump the Queen on you at any time.

difficulty.easy: Leads high cards blindly; forgets to follow suit; holds onto the Queen of Spades too long; doesn't track void suits.
difficulty.medium: Excellent suit-voiding strategy; tracks the Queen of Spades; understands when to slough high cards; avoids leading dangerous suits.
difficulty.hard: Expert at 'End-Play' manipulation; perfectly counts points; baits opponents into taking the 50-point penalty; optimal void creation timing; can execute 'shoot the moon' when opportunity arises.

considerations: Avoidance-based trick weighting (which tricks are 'safe' to win).

additional: Skat and Doppelkopf rulebooks (for 32-card deck usage)
